title: Trains to the Bronx
subtitle: Kraftwerk into electro, and on to Detroit
intro: Kraftwerk made electronic music in Düsseldorf. Follow it to a Bronx party record, electro, and then to three friends near Detroit who turned it into techno. Each place heard something different in the same German records.

steps.framing: Start with a German band and a Bronx DJ. 'Planet Rock' in 1982 took the melody of Kraftwerk's 'Trans-Europe Express' and the rhythm of their 'Numbers', without asking first, before anyone had settled the rules for borrowing like that. With a Japanese drum machine on top, it is the busiest crossing on the map.

The drums on the same record come from Roland's TR-808, a machine that had failed because it did not sound like a real drummer. On 'Planet Rock', sounding like a machine is the point: the 808's flaw became its value, and that is the electro sound this thread follows.
In Detroit, Juan Atkins was hearing Kraftwerk on the radio next to funk records like Parliament. He put the two together, and he named what he made techno.

Atkins had two friends from school in Belleville, Michigan: Derrick May and Kevin Saunderson, the Belleville Three. Atkins recorded and released music first, and May followed his example. The three men have told this story almost the same way for decades, which makes it one of the best-documented origin stories on the map. This stop is dated 1981, two years before the last one, so the timeline steps back a little.

Saunderson watched Atkins put out his own records on his own label, Metroplex, and later started his own, KMS. He has said that Atkins's example, not only his music, was the model. The music came with a way of working: make it yourself and release it yourself.

outro: The same records meant different things in different places. In the Bronx they were party music. In Detroit they became the start of a new kind of music, recorded, released and named by the people who made it.
